newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians prepare for another Israeli pullback.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians prepare for another Israeli pullback.

text.p: Palestinians in Halhoul prepared on Thursday to take control of their West Bank town as the Israeli cabinet convened to debate handing over more land under a peace deal with the PLO.

Halhoul, home to 25,000 Arabs and known for its fervent resistance to Israeli military occupation, is expected to be included in the area Israeli forces leave in the first of three pullbacks from mainly rural regions.
While waiting for Israel's cabinet to decide on the scope of the first redeployment, Halhul residents decorated their town with Palestinian flags and pictures of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Residents defied the cold to slap fresh coats of paint on shops as municipal workers cleared piles of rubble and dirt from streets.
"We are very happy because the Israeli occupation will end and we will be governed by our own people," said 53-year-old Azmi Abu Asbeh, as he painted his carpentry supplies store.
Ashraf Ali Milhem, 15, said: "We are going to be free. We will not see Israeli soldiers anymore."
The town, straddling the main Hebron-Jerusalem road used by Jewish settlers, is famous for lush vineyards that grace the valleys around its stone houses.

But it has also been a hotbed of Palestinian nationalism and the site of almost daily clashes between Arab stone-throwers and Israeli soldiers during a six-year uprising that erupted in the West Bank and Gaza in 1987.
Israeli troops have already left seven Arab cities in the West Bank and most of Hebron under a 1995 self-rule accord.
Israeli troops kept Palestinians in Halhoul under check with military observation points and two army camps that were dismantled last year after Israel built a detour road skirting the town.
A red sign in Hebrew and Arabic at the southern entrance of the town defines Halhoul as being under "Israeli security control".

In 1980, Israel expelled the town's mayor, Mohammad Milhem, to Lebanon in reprisal for a Palestinian guerrilla attack in neighbouring Hebron in which several settlers were killed. Milhem returned home in 1996 and resumed his mayoral duties.
Many Halhoul residents said that even after the Israelis pull out, their freedom will still be incomplete.
"We want not only Halhoul to be free, but all the Palestinian lands," said Sami Karajeh, 45.
"Right now, our country is divided into cantons. Our true freedom will be when we establish our independent state and fly our flag over Jerusalem," he said.
